newsitem.title: GERMANY: Daimler roars back to profit in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Daimler roars back to profit in 1996.

text.p: German industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG on Wednesday announced a convincing return to profitability in 1996 after posting the largest loss in German corporate history in 1995.

Germany's largest company, which owns automaker Mercedes-Benz, said in a brief statement that 1996 net income climbed to 2.8 billion German marks ($1.7 billion), up from a 5.7 billion-mark ($3.38 billion) loss the year before.
Daimler said the improved results would allow it to pay a dividend of 1.10 marks (65 cents) per share after failing to pay a dividend in 1995 for the first time in over four decades.

Analysts were surprised at the size of Daimler's net profit, which they said was based on strong sales at its Mercedes-Benz car and truck unit and a smaller loss at aircraft unit Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (DASA).
"The net income figure was clearly higher than expected," said Geroge Stuerzer, analyst at Vereinsbank Research in Munich. "Profits should climb again this year."

The improving bottom line came as welcome news for Daimler Chairman Juergen Schrempp, who has made "shareholder value" a personal mission, reshaping Daimler and setting clear profit targets for each operating unit.
Sales climbed to 106.3 billion marks ($63.05 billion) in 1996 from 103.55 billion marks ($61.42 billion) the year before.
Daimler stock surged in after-market trade to an all-time high of 136.00 marks ($80.66) after the announcement before closing at 135.80 ($80.55), a 4.5 percent gain on the day.

Wednesday's figures marked a sharp turnaround from record losses in 1995, which came largely as Schrempp slashed unprofitable businesses and took billions of marks worth of writedowns that he said were needed to make the company more profitable in the future.
In two controversial moves, Daimler cut off support for Dutch aircraft unit Fokker NV, sending it into bankruptcy, and dissolved its rail and engineering unit AEG.
The moves left Daimler to more closely focus on its transportation roots, especially car and truck making unit Mercedes-Benz.
Daimler's profit figures are a vindication of sorts for Schrempp, who has been criticised by unions and others for making sweeping changes.

In addition to dumping some businesses, Schrempp earlier this year technically closed Daimler's Mercedes-Benz car unit, absorbing it into the company structure and slashing layers of middle management.
